extracted.intended_audience: university faculty, administrators, and scholars debating the role of theology in higher education
extracted.subtask_description: Arguments and evaluative principles about whether and how Theology (natural and revealed) should be included in a university's curriculum, and about the proper relation between Theology and other branches of knowledge, arts, and sciences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theology as necessary for completeness of University teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: To withdraw Theology from the public schools is to impair the completeness and to invalidate the trustworthiness of all that is actually taught in them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the branches of knowledge hang together so that none can be neglected without prejudice to the rest, and if Theology is a branch of knowledge of wide reception and philosophical structure, then omitting Theology mutilates the circle of knowledge; Religious Truth is not only a portion but a condition of general knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat Theology as a precise and consistent intellectual structure
rubrics_metrics.description: When I speak of Theism or Monotheism, I am not throwing together discordant doctrines... I speak of one idea unfolded in its just proportions, carried out upon an intelligible method, and issuing in necessary and immutable results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theology should not be treated as a shapeless aggregate of opinions; it should be taught and judged as a coherent science with an intelligible method rather than a mere medley of beliefs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wide historical reception justifies inclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Theology... has had a place, if not possession, in the intellectual world from time immemorial; it has been received by minds the most various, and in systems of religion the most hostile to each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The universality of theological ideas across ages, cultures, and major authors (Bacon, Newton, Berkeley, Butler, Shakespeare, Milton, etc.) gives Theology prima facie claims to be entertained within university instruction rather than ignored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural theology informs other disciplines and must be considered
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural Theology... cannot fail, considered as knowledge, to exert a powerful influence on philosophy, literature, and every intellectual creation or discovery whatever.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophy, history, ethics, physics, metaphysics, and political science may all be traversed by theological considerations; inquiry into many results should include what Theology has to say about them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revealed religion furnishes facts and corrects secular science
rubrics_metrics.description: Revealed Religion furnishes facts to the other sciences, which those sciences, left to themselves, would never reach; and it invalidates apparent facts, which, left to themselves, they would imagine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: historical facts (Noah's Ark) that secular history would not discover; Revelation may contradict plausible scientific inferences (e.g., about human perfectibility) and thus must be taken into account where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: A University of universal knowledge must explicitly accept or reprobate Theology
rubrics_metrics.description: It cannot be passed over in a scheme of universal instruction, without involving a positive denial of its truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a scheme of universal instruction claims completeness, it cannot omit Theology as a neutral omission; the institution must either include theological teaching or explicitly reject it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid disciplinary overreach: sciences must not be sole exponents of all truth
rubrics_metrics.description: No science whatever... will fall largely into error, if it be constituted the sole exponent of all things in heaven and earth, and that, for the simple reason that it is encroaching on territory not its own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclusive cultivation of any secular science can become dangerous by attempting to answer questions beyond its instruments; maintain methodological limits and resist treating one discipline as the arbiter of all questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent perversion by specialists who generalize beyond their scope ('man of one idea')
rubrics_metrics.description: Men... whose life lies in the cultivation of one science... often have absolute conviction of their own conclusions... Thus he becomes... a man of one idea... principles all of them true to a certain point, yet all degenerating into error and quackery, because they are carried to excess.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of elevating a partial truth into a universal key; examples include turning principles of anatomy, phrenology, utility, or progress into overarching philosophies; cultivate breadth and cross-disciplinary restraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other sciences will seize theology's place if Theology is omitted
rubrics_metrics.description: If you drop any science out of the circle of knowledge, you cannot keep its place vacant for it; that science is forgotten; the other sciences close up, or... they exceed their proper bounds, and intrude where they have no right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omission leads to misplacement of subject-matter (e.g., history absorbed by metaphysics), producing errors because the usurping sciences lack the instruments to teach that territory rightly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fine Arts should be handmaids of Religion when addressing sacred themes
rubrics_metrics.description: These high ministers of the Beautiful and the Noble are... special attendants and handmaids of Religion; but they are apt to forget their place, and, unless restrained with a firm hand, instead of being servants, will aim at becoming principals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When painting, music, or architecture engage sacred subjects they must serve religious ends and not make Religion subordinate to artistic aims; otherwise sacred subjects risk being treated as natural or pagan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artists must subordinate personal genius to sacred scholarship when serving Religion
rubrics_metrics.description: If he would do honour to the highest of subjects, he must make himself its scholar, must humbly follow the thoughts given him, and must aim at the glory, not of his own gift, but of the Great Giver.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artists/composers working on Masses, Offices, or sacred iconography should study the religious content and priorities and avoid using religion merely as material for personal display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution about revivals and liturgical/rubrical anachronism
rubrics_metrics.description: That revival of an almost forgotten architecture... may in some way or other run away with us into this or that error... an obsolete discipline may be a present heresy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admiration for Gothic or other revival styles must be tempered by awareness of current social conditions and the risk that a revived style might carry inappropriate political or ceremonial connotations; rubrics have been altered to meet the times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholars should be modest in pronouncements outside their field
rubrics_metrics.description: Men whose life lies in the cultivation of one science... have no more right, though they have often more ambition, to generalize upon the basis of their own pursuit but beyond its range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid confident public generalizations by specialists on subjects where they lack competence; such temperance prevents inadvertent undermining of other disciplines (including Theology).
